newsitem.title: USA: Study links AIDS drug to CMV retinitis.
newsitem.headline: Study links AIDS drug to CMV retinitis.

text.p: The same drug that has been successful in suppressing the AIDS virus could also trigger the onset of CMV retinitis, an eye disease that can lead to blindness, researchers said on Thursday.

Researchers have long known of the link between AIDS and CMV retinitis, which strikes about 40 percent of advanced AIDS patients. But the new findings suggest that protease inhibitor drugs may actually cause the eye disease to appear in healthier AIDS patients as well.

The results were reported by researchers at the University of California at San Francisco, who published their findings last month in the British medical journal, Lancet. Their study involved just five patients, but they said data from other studies supported their findings.
Before the protease inhibitor became a commonly prescribed AIDS drug, doctors rarely saw CMV retinitis in patients before their immune, or T cell count dropped below 50.

"Now we have found that patients can have counts well over 100 and still develop CMV retinitis and that it might be triggered by taking protease inhibitors," said Dr. Mark Jacobson, associate professor of medicine at the University and author of the study.

A normal T cell count in a healty person is about 400, but that number falls as the AIDS virus progresses. Patients however, remain relatively healthy with counts of 200 and generally do not see most serious side effects until it drops below 50.

It is not understood why protease inhibitors might cause CMV retinitis to strike healthier patients, but doctors say they suspect the infection in the eye may take root earlier than thought and lie dormant for some time. If this were the case, Jacobson said, drugs that boost the immune system could make more T cells available to fight this eye infection, perhaps leading to an inflammatory response that brings on full-blown CMV retinitis.

Even if a clear link between protease inhibitors and CMV retinitis were to be established, Jacobson said that would in no way suggest the drug should be avoided since its benefits far outweigh associated risks. When combined with other AIDS drugs, protease inhibitors are part of a highly effective AIDS treatment that has helped drive down the virus to nondetectable levels in thousands of patients.
But he added that doctors should be aware of the increased risk of CMV retinitis, which can be successfully treated if it is detected early enough.
